---
title: "Are Americans leaving work, or just getting older?"
subtitle: "US labor-force participation is down four points since 1990. Splitting it into behavior and age structure shows which one did it."
author: "Kyle Tong"
date: 2026-09-28
categories:
  - labor market
  - data visualization
  - IPUMS CPS
description: "Participation is down four points since 1990. It is up inside every age group over 25. The difference is the age structure of the country."
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(here)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))

AGE_COLOURS <- c("16-24" = "#D55E00", "25-54" = "#0072B2",
                 "55-64" = "#009E73", "65+"   = "#CC79A7")

DERIVED <- here("blog", "posts", "post3", "data", "derived")

lfp <- read_csv(file.path(DERIVED, "lfp_by_age.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(age_group = factor(age_group, levels = names(AGE_COLOURS)))

gap <- read_csv(file.path(DERIVED, "weighting_gap.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

base <- lfp |>
  filter(year == 1990) |>
  select(age_group, lfp_1990 = lfp, share_1990 = share)

# Shift-share. "Rates only" lets participation move with age shares frozen at
# 1990; "shares only" lets the age structure move with 1990 participation.
agg <- lfp |>
  left_join(base, by = "age_group") |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(actual      = sum(share * lfp),
            rates_only  = sum(share_1990 * lfp),
            shares_only = sum(share * lfp_1990),
            .groups     = "drop")

pick <- function(df, col, yr) 100 * df[[col]][df$year == yr]
pct  <- function(x, d = 1) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)
grp  <- function(g, yr) 100 * lfp$lfp[lfp$age_group == g & lfp$year == yr]
shr  <- function(g, yr) 100 * lfp$share[lfp$age_group == g & lfp$year == yr]
```

The share of Americans aged 16 and over who are working or looking for work fell from
`r pct(pick(agg, "actual", 1990))` percent in March 1990 to
`r pct(pick(agg, "actual", 2026))` percent in March 2026. A four-point fall sounds like a lot
of people giving up on work.

The question this post answers is: **did participation fall because Americans of a given
age became less likely to work, or because more Americans are now at ages when people
usually do not work?** The first would be a labor-market problem. The second is
demographic arithmetic that no labor-market policy can undo.

The national rate is a weighted average of age-group rates,

$$\text{LFP}_t = \sum_a s_{a,t} \, p_{a,t},$$

where $p_{a,t}$ is participation in age group $a$ and $s_{a,t}$ is that group's share of the
adult population. It can fall because the $p$'s fall (behavior) or because the $s$'s shift
toward low-participation groups (composition). The three charts take these in turn:
@fig-groups shows the rates, @fig-shares the shares, and @fig-decomp recombines them to see
which one moved the total.

## The data

Every March Basic Monthly sample from IPUMS CPS, 1990 to 2026, with age, labor-force
status and the person weight `WTFINL`. Every rate and share is weighted:

```{r}
#| label: weighting
#| eval: false

adults |>
  group_by(year, age_group) |>
  summarise(lfp        = weighted.mean(in_lf, wtfinl),
            population = sum(wtfinl))
```

The universe is people 16 and over with `LABFORCE` in `(1, 2)`. Weighting matters here:
the unweighted rate for March 2026 is `r pct(100 * gap$unweighted[gap$year == 2026])`
percent against a weighted `r pct(100 * gap$weighted[gap$year == 2026])`, because people
over 65 are `r pct(100 * sum(lfp$n[lfp$year == 2026 & lfp$age_group == "65+"]) / sum(lfp$n[lfp$year == 2026]))`
percent of the interviewed sample and `r pct(shr("65+", 2026))` percent of the population.
Older people answer the survey more often, which is exactly the group this post is about.

## Did behavior change? Participation by age

```{r}
#| label: fig-groups
#| fig-cap: "The behavior piece: weighted labor-force participation by age group, March of each year. Every group over 25 ends above where it started."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| echo: false

ggplot(lfp, aes(year, lfp, colour = age_group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = AGE_COLOURS, name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "labor-force participation") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Workers aged 25 to 54 participate at `r pct(grp("25-54", 2026))` percent, against
`r pct(grp("25-54", 1990))` percent in 1990. The 55 to 64 group went from
`r pct(grp("55-64", 1990))` to `r pct(grp("55-64", 2026))` percent, and participation
after 65 rose from `r pct(grp("65+", 1990))` to `r pct(grp("65+", 2026))` percent. The one
group that pulled back is the youngest, down
`r pct(grp("16-24", 1990) - grp("16-24", 2026))` points, probably mostly school
enrollment, which this extract cannot confirm. On the
behavioral side, then, the answer is no: past age 25, people work more than they did in
1990.

## Did the population change? Age shares

```{r}
#| label: fig-shares
#| fig-cap: "The composition piece: share of the population aged 16 and over, by age group. The 65+ group, which participates least, gained eight points."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| echo: false

ggplot(lfp, aes(year, share, colour = age_group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = AGE_COLOURS, name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "share of adult population") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

People over 65 were `r pct(shr("65+", 1990))` percent of the adult population in 1990 and
are `r pct(shr("65+", 2026))` percent now. The prime-age group fell from
`r pct(shr("25-54", 1990))` to `r pct(shr("25-54", 2026))` percent. Since participation
after 65 is around a fifth and participation between 25 and 54 is above four fifths, that
reshuffling pulls the national average down on its own, without anyone changing their mind
about work. On the composition side, the answer is yes.

## Which one moved the total?

```{r}
#| label: fig-decomp
#| fig-cap: "Putting them together: actual participation and two counterfactuals. The dashed line keeps 1990 age shares (behavior only); the dotted line keeps 1990 rates (aging only)."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
#| echo: false

agg |>
  pivot_longer(-year) |>
  mutate(name = factor(name, levels = c("actual", "rates_only", "shares_only"),
                       labels = c("actual",
                                  "1990 age shares, actual rates",
                                  "actual age shares, 1990 rates"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, value, colour = name, linetype = name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey20", "#0072B2", "#D55E00"), name = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed", "dotted"), name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "participation rate, 16 and over") +
  theme(legend.position = "top", legend.text = element_text(size = 9)) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2), linetype = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
```

Freeze the age structure at its 1990 shares and let participation move as it actually did:
the rate ends at `r pct(pick(agg, "rates_only", 2026))` percent, slightly above where it
started. Freeze participation instead and let only the age structure move: the rate falls
to `r pct(pick(agg, "shares_only", 2026))` percent. The entire decline in the headline
number, and more, is demographics.

The actual line sits above the aging-only line because the groups gaining population share
are the ones raising their participation: older Americans working longer has offset about
`r pct(pick(agg, "actual", 2026) - pick(agg, "shares_only", 2026))` points of what aging
would otherwise have taken out.

## What the three charts say together

@fig-groups rules out the behavioral story for everyone over 25. @fig-shares shows the
population moving toward the age group with the lowest participation. @fig-decomp shows that
this shift alone accounts for the whole decline: with the 1990 age mix, participation today
would be higher than it was in 1990. Americans are not leaving work; the country is getting
older.

Two lessons follow. The headline rate is a poor gauge of labor-market health, because it
falls whenever the population ages; the prime-age rate in @fig-groups, now
`r pct(grp("25-54", 2026))` percent and within
`r pct(100 * max(lfp$lfp[lfp$age_group == "25-54"]) - grp("25-54", 2026))` points of its
`r lfp$year[lfp$age_group == "25-54"][which.max(lfp$lfp[lfp$age_group == "25-54"])]` peak,
is the better signal. And because the youngest baby boomers do not turn 65 until 2029, the
headline rate will probably keep drifting down even if every age group keeps working as much
as it does now. A falling participation rate in the next few years should not, by itself, be
read as Americans giving up on work.

## Caveats

Each point is one March, so 2021 carries the pandemic. Census-based reweighting leaves
small breaks around 2000, 2010 and 2020. And a shift-share split is an accounting identity:
it locates the change in the age structure but does not explain why 60-year-olds now work
more.

Scripts are in `R/` and details in `README.md`; the raw extract stays out of the
repository, and `01_acquire.R` rebuilds it with an IPUMS account.
